opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the simplest way right now is almost embarrassingly straightforward: collect a lot of teleoperated demonstrations and train an end-to-end policy on them with imitation learning.

You set up a bimanual system, two arms with grippers and a few cameras, maybe one on each wrist and one overhead. A person drives the robot through a leader-follower setup or some teleop interface and folds the shirt, again and again. You record the camera images and joint actions, then train a neural network, these days often a transformer with a diffusion or flow-matching action head, to map what it sees to what it should do next, predicting short chunks of actions at a time.

What surprised a lot of people, including me, is how far that gets you. A few years ago folding was the classic "this is impossible" task for robotics. Cloth is deformable, the state space is basically infinite, and you can't easily model it the way you'd model a rigid object. People spent years on cloth simulation and hand-designed perception pipelines that tried to find the corners and the collar. The data-driven approach sidesteps all of that. The network doesn't need an explicit model of the shirt. It just learns, from enough examples, that when the cloth looks like this, you grab here and pull that way.

There are caveats. "Simplest" doesn't mean "easy." Data quality matters enormously. If your operators are inconsistent, the policy gets confused. Diversity matters too: different shirts, colors, starting crumples, lighting. And the hardest part usually isn't the clean fold in the middle. It's the beginning, flattening a crumpled pile, and recovering from mistakes. That's where you need the data to include corrections, or you need some reinforcement learning or other fine-tuning on top.

Pretraining also helps. If you start from a model trained on lots of robot data across many tasks, you need far fewer folding demos, and the result is more robust. But if someone asked me, "I have two arms and a month, what do I do?", I'd say: build a good teleop setup, collect a few hundred high-quality demos, and train a diffusion-style policy. You'll probably get something that folds a shirt surprisingly well.

r001.rationale: It recommends collecting teleoperated demonstrations from the robot and training an imitation-learning policy as the simplest current approach.

r002.rationale: It mentions pretraining on robot data, but does not propose starting with an existing open-source model to collect clothes-folding data.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the simplest way right now is still imitation learning with a lot of teleoperated demonstrations. You put a human on a teleop rig, you have them fold a few thousand pieces of clothing with the robot's own arms and the robot's own cameras, and then you train a policy to map what the camera sees to what the arms should do. No physics simulation, no explicit cloth model, no hand-written state machine. It sounds almost too dumb, but it works, and it works better than almost everything we tried the "clever" way for the past fifteen years.

The reason it works is that folding clothes is a problem where the hard part is perception and contact, not planning. Cloth is deformable, it has basically infinite degrees of freedom, and you can't write down its state in a way that's useful. So any approach that tries to estimate the state first and then plan on top of it gets stuck immediately. But a human doesn't think about cloth state either. They just look, grab a corner, pull, and respond to what happens. When you collect demonstrations, you're capturing that reactive behavior directly, and a reasonably sized model with enough data will pick up that closed-loop skill.

There are a few practical things that matter more than people expect. One is the embodiment: two arms are enormously easier than one, because most folding is really a "hold here, move there" operation, and with a single arm you end up doing a lot of awkward regrasps. Second is the gripper. A simple parallel-jaw gripper with soft fingertips is fine. You do not need a dexterous hand. Third is data diversity. If you only fold one t-shirt on one table, the policy will fail the moment the lighting changes. You want many garments, many starting states, different colors, crumpled, inside out, all of it.

And you have to be a little honest about what "simplest" means. It's conceptually simple, but it's not cheap. The bottleneck has shifted from algorithm design to data collection and operations. Running a teleop setup for weeks, keeping it consistent, labeling failures, that's real work. The flip side is that it's very predictable work. You know that more good data generally gives you a better policy, and that's a trade you can plan a project around.

The more interesting question is what comes after. The pre-trained vision-language-action models are starting to make this even simpler because you start from a model that already roughly knows what a shirt is and what "fold" means, and then you only need a few hundred demonstrations instead of thousands. That's where I think it's going. But if someone asked me today, with a robot in the lab and a month of time, I'd tell them to go collect demonstrations and train a diffusion or transformer policy. It's the boring answer, and it's the right one.

r001.rationale: It identifies teleoperated demonstrations collected with the robot’s own arms and cameras as the simplest current approach.

r002.rationale: It mentions starting from pretrained vision-language-action models, but does not identify them as open-source models.

astra-6.text: I’d start by making the task very constrained: one type of garment, laid flat on a table, with a fixed camera and a simple folding sequence. If you mean the quickest way to get a demonstration working, you could have a person teleoperate the robot. Then use those demonstrations to teach it to repeat the task. The tricky part is taking a crumpled shirt from a pile, figuring out where everything is, and recovering when a grasp goes wrong. So I’d solve the folding first and gradually add that variability.

r001.rationale: The response suggests teleoperating the robot and using demonstrations, but does not clearly identify collecting real-robot data as the simplest current approach.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose starting from an existing open-source model.

sol-6.1.text: I think the simplest way right now is to make the task very constrained. Start with one type of clothing, like a T-shirt, laid flat on a table in roughly the same position. Then teach the robot a fixed sequence: grab here, fold this side, fold the other side, and fold the bottom up. You can add a camera to adjust where it grabs. Going from a pile of tangled laundry to neatly folded clothes is a much harder problem, so I’d start with that controlled setup.
